_meta.directives: Fiche recentrée sur le nom (2026-10-03). Chaque piste d'origine est attribuée à qui la porte et citée à la page dans les notes de sa source ; aucune n'est retenue comme la bonne. Ne pas étendre sans source dédiée.

oralTraditions.claim: A Kaagoro family narrative recounts that the Saagonè and the Daabo, "all Jaawara", that is, all Diawara, fought one another in the Kingui, and that the Kaagoro Ganyi Maamadu, born of the same mother as the Jaawara Jugudu Maamudu, helped his brother. The narrative does not say where the name comes from. The historian who publishes it concludes, with other studies, that the Kaagoro fought against the Daabo and that the Saagonè prevailed around 1753-1754.
oralTraditions.carrier: Tanba Dancogo, qui transmet une tradition familiale kaagoro du Baakhunu, au Mali
oralTraditions.context: Narrative collected in the Baakhunu, translated into French and published in 1988

writtenChronicles.claim: Souleymane Kanté, a Guinean author writing in Maninka and the inventor of the N'ko script, makes the Dabo the second branch of the Diawara, the first being the Sagonè. In his work on the clan names of the Manden, a war between the two branches, dated to the 300s of his calendar counted from the Kurukan Fuga assembly, drives part of the Dabo from their country of Baakhunu to the land of Sanan, between Kayes and Kinkin, probably the Kingui. There, he says, their name became Dabo, and their praise name became Sangan or Sanganjan. The same work says of the Diawara that they adopted the Soninke language after being subjugated by Soninke. It then has the Dabo move to the Fouta Djallon, where they take part in the battle of Talansa, around 1727, and then in the holy war alongside the Fulani, and attributes to them the founding of Dabola, from which they are said to have been driven out towards Kurukodo.

linguisticReconstructions.claim: No dictionary or study consulted gives a meaning for the word: the dictionary of Mandingo clan names defines Daabo only as a clan name, and the work written in N'ko that tells how some Diawara became Dabo does not say what the word means.

The name is written Daabo, with a long vowel, in the dictionary of Mandingo clan names and in the narratives of Baakhunu. In The Gambia, a catalogue entry from the national archives associates the spellings Darboe, Daboe, Darbo and Dabo with the name Daabo.

The dictionary of Mandinka clan names links Daabo to three groups: the Malinke; the Kagoro, for whom it gives the status of hɔ́rɔn (free person); and the Mandinka, for whom it gives the praise name Sonka.

Contributors to a Soninke community forum list Dabo among names of Soninke origin, and a Soninke community list cites Daabo as the second name (jammu kare) of Mangasuba. These lists say nothing about the origin of the word.
A country called the Dabo borders the Baakhunu to the south. No source consulted says whether this place name and the clan name are related.

The name is thus linked to the Malinke, the Kagoro and the Mandinka on one side, and through the Diawara to the Soninke world on the other. These links say who bears the name, not where the word comes from: the origin of the name is not established.

homonyms.label: Dabo, au Kano
homonyms.distinction: In Kano, in the north of present-day Nigeria, Dabo is the name of Ibrahim Dabo, the second Fulani emir of Kano, from 1819 to 1846, one of whose sons, Abdullah, was the fourth emir. The Kano Chronicle celebrates him as "Dabo, sacker of towns" without explaining the name. No source consulted links it to the Mandingo clan name, or says which of the two the Dabo of Nigeria bear: this is why Nigeria is given here only as presumed.

sources.title: Bamadaba — dictionnaire des noms claniques (jamuw)
sources.notes: Appendix of clan names of the Bamadaba, an electronic Bambara-French dictionary of the Corpus bambara de référence (Bailleul, Davydov, Erman, Maslinsky, Méric, Vydrin, 2011-2020, CC BY-NC-SA), noted by Vydrin in Mandenkan 63, 2020, pp. 89-110. Complete file consulted. The Daabo entry gives the variant Dabo, three bearing groups (Malinke, Kagoro, Mandinka), the hɔ́rɔn status among the Kagoro and the praise name Sonka among the Mandinka; it gives no meaning for the name. The groups are read from the corresponding entry in Bogacheva's thesis, which names them in full. The Gèyita entry cites Daabɔ among its joking partners. The entry names no country.

sources.title: Les noms de famille avec leur jammu kare
sources.notes: Soninke community portal, social organisation page with no identified academic author: a non-exhaustive list, compiled by the portal's users, of the second names (jammu kare) given to Soninke family names. The jammu kare is, the page says, the second name added to a family name and serving as its identifier. Consulted in an archived copy of 12 December 2024. Only the presence of the name in the list and its second names are taken from it: the list says nothing about their origin.

sources.title: Les noms de Famille d'Origine Soninké
sources.notes: Discussion thread on the forum of the community portal Soninkara.com, opened in December 2006 and continued until 2011: contributors, under pseudonyms, compile lists of names they consider Soninke. The lists partly overlap and contradict one another: several participants point out that many names borne today by Soninke are not originally Soninke, and one of them asks that Soninke names be distinguished from names of Soninke origin. Consulted in an archived copy from 2024.

sources.title: Dabo — origine, signification et incidence du nom de famille
sources.notes: Worldwide genealogy aggregator, consulted on 29 September 2026. Worldwide incidence of about 148,045 bearers; Mali 28,782, Senegal 26,247, Guinea-Bissau 20,598, Nigeria 16,545, Guinea 13,504, Burkina Faso 7,974. The page gives no meaning for the name. Figures for outside Africa are not included in the attestations of this fiche.

sources.title: Les noms de clan du Manden (jamu) dans les sources africaines, occidentales et arabes
sources.notes: Bogacheva, E. A., bachelor's thesis, Saint Petersburg State University, 2017, in Russian; supervised by A. Davydov, reviewed by V. Vydrin. Daabo entry, pp. 24-25: the variant Dabo, the Malinke, Kagoro and Mandinka as bearers, the hɔ́rɔn status among the Kagoro, the praise name sonka among the Mandinka, then the account drawn from Souleymane Kanté's N'ko work on the kinds of si and jamu of the Manden: the split between Sagonè and Dabo, the land of Sanan where the name becomes Dabo and the praise name Sangan or Sanganjan, the Fouta Djallon, Talansan and Dabola. Jáwara entry, p. 58: according to the same work, the Diawara have two branches, the Sagonè at Kinkin and the Dabo at Baakhunu, and adopted the Soninke language. Kanté's original N'ko text has not been read; only its Russian translation has, and its dates in years counted from the Kurukan Fuga assembly do not all agree. A bachelor's thesis is not a peer-reviewed publication: it is cited for the accounts it relays. Souleymane Kanté is presented there as the inventor of the N'ko script (p. 9).

sources.title: Une formation politique précoloniale du Sahel occidental malien : le Baakhunu à l'époque des Kaagoro
sources.notes: Ardouin, Claude-Daniel, Cahiers d'études africaines, volume 28, issue 111-112, 1988, pp. 443-461. Study based on oral traditions collected in the Baakhunu, in the west of the Malian Sahel. The Baakhunu bounded to the south by the Dabo (p. 443); the narrative of Tanba Dancogo: "The Saagonè and the Daabo, they are all Jaawara, fought" (p. 447); the Kaagoro present at Foose taking part in the internal struggle of the Jaawara against the Daabo (p. 448); the Saagonè victory over the Daabo around 1753-1754, according to Boyer 1953 and Diawara 1985 (p. 449).

sources.title: An Interview About The History of The Daabo Clan in Busumbala (NCAC_RDD_TAPE_2010A)
sources.notes: Catalogue entry for a recording in The Gambia's digital national archives (NCAC), published in 2023 by the University of Hamburg. The recording is under restricted access: we have read only the catalogue entry, which names the informant, Keemo Daabo of Busumbala, announces his origin, his migration and his genealogy, and gives among its search keywords the spellings Darboe, Daboe, Darbo and Dabo. Other entries in the same collection concern the Daabo of Gunjur and Basori; we have heard none of these interviews, which may contain a local narrative about the name.

sources.title: Histoire générale de l'Afrique, VI, ch. 22 : Le califat de Sokoto et le Borno
sources.notes: UNESCO, 1996; chapter by Murray Last. Printed page 620: the long civil war following the accession of the second emir of Kano, Ibrahim Dabo, and his 27-year reign, from 1819 to 1846; the fourth emir, Abdullah, son of Dabo. The chapter says nothing about the name itself.

sources.title: The Kano Chronicle
sources.notes: Palmer, H. R., Journal of the Royal Anthropological Institute, volume 38, 1908, pp. 58-98. English translation, by a British colonial administrator, of a chronicle of the rulers of Kano. Entry for Ibrahim Dabo, son of Mohammadu, forty-fifth ruler, and the song that calls him "sacker of towns" (pp. 95-96); entry for his son Osumanu (p. 96). The chronicle does not explain the name.

gaps.reason: We name no bearer: no source consulted cites one who is deceased and whose belonging to this clan name is established.
The dictionary of Mandingo clan names cites Daabɔ among the joking partners of the Gèyita clan; we have no fiche for this name, and we have found no other attested joking relationship for Dabo.
The dictionary of Mandinka clan names gives the status of free person (hɔ́rɔn) to the Kagoro Dabo, but no social function specific to the name: we infer no function from it.
